idiom_name: _Thread_local statics plus pthread TSD keys with a hand-written ownership discipline
implementation_notes: C provides per-thread storage but no confinement enforcement: C11 `_Thread_local` (spelled `thread_local` since C23, `__thread` as the GCC extension) gives file- and block-scope variables one instance per thread with automatic destruction at thread exit, while the POSIX TSD API (pthread_key_create plus pthread_setspecific/pthread_getspecific, one key per logical slot and a destructor for cleanup) is the portable mechanism for dynamically allocated per-thread data and the only option before C11. Both replace the hand-rolled per-thread registry with a compiler- or libc-managed slot, but confining an object graph - ensuring no reference ever reaches another thread - remains a hand-written discipline of private structs, ownership comments and message copying. The classic hand-off structure (a queue plus one worker that exclusively owns the data) is still justified when several threads must cooperate on long-lived state, because storage duration alone never makes sharing safe.
pitfalls: Dynamically allocated TSD must be released in the key's destructor; a key created with a NULL destructor leaks every thread's storage, and a destructor that re-associates a non-NULL value can loop through the implementation's retry limit.

`_Thread_local` at file scope needs `static` or `extern` (the specifier must agree across declarations), and in shared libraries every load can create additional instances with per-thread lazy initialization.
The compiler enforces storage, never ownership: copying a confined struct into a queue or a global hands other threads the live data, and that data race is undefined behaviour with no diagnostic.
